evidence.relevance_note: GRADE-based multi-society guideline giving a Strong recommendation for IM epinephrine as first-line, with explicit dosing and an explicit statement that antihistamines/glucocorticoids are NOT first-line. Independently corroborates the WAO recommendation.
evidence.text: Epinephrine is the first-line medicine in GRADE II to IV anaphylaxis (Strong recommendation). The recommended dose of IM epinephrine is 0.01 mg/kg, up to a maximum of 0.5 mg for patients aged >=14 years, and up to a maximum of 0.3 mg in patients <14 years old. Epinephrine concentration should be 1 mg/ml (1:1000). H1 antagonists and glucocorticoids are second-line medications and are not a substitute for epinephrine.
evidence.title: A Clinical Practice Guideline for the Emergency Management of Anaphylaxis (2020)

evidence.relevance_note: Peak Australasian specialist body; states IM adrenaline is first-line with identical dosing (0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg, 1:1000, outer mid-thigh) and that steroids/antihistamines are not first-line. Third independent confirmation.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: confident, accurate, cites all three packet sources with exact concordant figures.
fixed_stress_answers.text: The recommended first-line pharmacologic treatment for anaphylaxis is intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline). The World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020 states that 'intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline) continues to be the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis,' given into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh) at 0.01 mg/kg of body weight, to a maximum total dose of 0.5 mg, using the 1 mg/mL (1:1000) concentration, repeatable every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist [wao_2020]. This is independently corroborated by the Frontiers in Pharmacology 2022 clinical practice guideline, which gives a Strong recommendation that 'epinephrine is the first-line medicine,' at 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg (max 0.3 mg for patients <14 years), 1 mg/mL [fphar_2022], and by the ASCIA 2024 guideline, which states 'adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first line treatment' at 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg, 1:1000, into the outer mid-thigh [ascia_2024]. All three explicitly note that antihistamines and corticosteroids are NOT first-line and are not substitutes for epinephrine.

ground_truth.answer: The first-line pharmacologic treatment for anaphylaxis is intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline). Per the World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance 2020 and corroborating guidelines, it is given by the intramuscular route into the mid-anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis) at a dose of 0.01 mg/kg of body weight, up to a maximum total dose of 0.5 mg, using the 1 mg/mL (1:1000) concentration. (The Frontiers in Pharmacology 2022 guideline adds a child maximum of 0.3 mg for patients <14 years.) The dose may be repeated every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist. Antihistamines and glucocorticoids are explicitly NOT first-line and are not substitutes for epinephrine.
ground_truth.why_answerable: All three guidelines state, in unambiguous language, that intramuscular epinephrine/adrenaline is the single first-line drug, and they give concordant exact figures (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg, 1 mg/mL [1:1000], anterolateral thigh). There is no conflict among the sources, and the dosing is numerically consistent.
